messages.author: df2ff87426a98fc9
messages.subject: Double Observer Detection Probabilities
parts:
I surveyed a sample of wetlands for grebes by making a single visiting
and recording whether I detected a grebe during the first minute (of
silence) or during the second minute (during which I played a grebe
call). I am primarily interested in estimating grebe occupancy (P/A
data, not abundance) and detection probability and I wonder if I could
use the gmultmix() function to do so in a dependent double observer
context. Ideally, I would estimate:

1) separate detection probabilities for each method (one minute of
silence, one minute of call playbacks), and

2) also for the combined protocol involving both methods.

I can't find any reference to such an analysis in the unmarked
documentation, so hope you might shed some light on the matter.

Cheers,
Dan

messages.author: 527e14923215b7e4
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Double Observer Detection Probabilities
parts:
Hi Dan,

I think you can use either multinomPois() or gmultmix() to analyze your data, but can you clarify a few things first.

1) Did you ever detect >1 bird at a point, and if so did you record the data as counts? Or did you just record binary detection/non-detection data?
2) Were there two observers,  or just one?
3) If you detected a bird in both time intervals, did you record that, or did you just record the first detection?

Richard

messages.author: df2ff87426a98fc9
messages.subject: Re: Double Observer Detection Probabilities
parts:
Hi Richard,

To answer your questions:
1) Yes, often there are 2 birds (a pair) detected at a wetland, but
there is rarely >2. And yes, I did record the count. I assumed that
because the count is generally 1 or 2, that I could collapse the data
into P/A for simplicity. However, if unmarked requires me to use count
data I can go that route.
2) A single observer.
3) If a bird was detected in both time intervals, then I recorded it
in both.

Cheers,
Dan

Once you estimate abundance, it is easy to convert that to an estimate of occupancy.

messages.author: 527e14923215b7e4
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Double Observer Detection Probabilities
parts:
Hi Dan,

I think you want the independent double observer method, which has the following cell probs:

"10" = p1 * (1-p2)  # detected in first time interval, but not in second
"01" =  (1-p1) * p2 # detected in second time interval, but not in first
"11" = p1 * p2        # detected in both time intervals

Someone please correct me if I'm wrong.

You need to use count data, but it's no problem if it turns out that you don't have any values > 1 in the y matrix. Just make sure that you don't convert integers >1 to 1. Once you estimate lambda, you can obtain an estimate of occurrence probability using the equation:

psi = 1 - exp(-lambda)

Richard

Thanks for pointing me in the right direction. I have been following
the example you suggested and have run into an error when I try to run
a model (see reproducible example below). Any idea of how I can
correct this?

Cheers,
Dan


# Simulate Data #
y.1<-round(rnorm(mean=3,n=50,sd=1.15))
y.2<-round(rnorm(mean=3,n=50,sd=1.15))
y<-data.frame(y.1,y.2)

nSites<- 50
observer <- matrix(c('A','B'), nSites, 2, byrow=TRUE)

# Construct UMF #
umf <- unmarkedFrameMPois(y=y, obsCovs=list(observer=observer),
type="double")

# Fit Model #
fm <- multinomPois(~observer-1 ~1, umf)

number of rows of result is not a multiple of vector length (arg 1)

messages.author: 527e14923215b7e4
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Double Observer Detection Probabilities
parts:
Hi Dan,

y should have 3 columns.

Column 1 is the number of birds detected in interval 1 but not in interval 2.
Column 2 is the number of birds detected in interval 2 but not in interval 1.
Column 3 is the number of birds detected in both intervals.

Take a look at the example again.

Richard
